---
title: "Modeling and documentation conventions"
subtitle: "One engine, shared equations, traceable assumptions"
---

MLSysIM is the modeling engine for the four-volume ML Systems textbook series.
The books are its primary integration consumers; the same public API also serves
students, instructors, and engineers working independently of the books.
Organize the engine by the system being modeled, not by volume or chapter.
A memory equation can serve a single accelerator, a fleet, an agent, or a robot.

## Follow a calculation through the code

| Layer | Question it answers | Location |
|---|---|---|
| Definitions | What hardware, workload, and environment are we modeling? | Registry packages and their `data/` directories |
| Physics | What equation applies, and where does it come from? | `mlsysim/physics/` |
| Solvers | How do the equations combine under these constraints? | `mlsysim/engine/solvers/` |
| Scenarios | What named configuration are we evaluating? | `mlsysim/engine/scenario_catalog/` and `scenario_definitions/` |
| Results | What does the answer mean, in which units? | `mlsysim/engine/result_types/` |
| Teaching | How does a reader reason about the result? | Quarto guides, textbook cells, and labs |

Keep equations in one implementation. A solver composes equations and checks
constraints; a scenario supplies inputs. Chapter-specific empirical series and
one-off anecdotes remain with the chapter rather than becoming engine constants.

Use descriptive names such as `context_tokens` and `bytes_per_element`. Short
symbols are appropriate when the adjacent docstring maps them directly to a
published equation. Keep units attached until formatting the output.

Split a large module when its domains can be understood independently. Preserve
public import paths through explicit re-exports, and compare outputs before and
after a move. Keep structural changes separate from changes to equations or defaults.

## Document the calculation where it lives

Use NumPy-style docstrings for public equations and solver methods. The first
sentence explains the purpose in plain English. Include these standard sections:

| Section | Required explanation |
|---|---|
| `Parameters` | Meaning, units, valid range, and meaning of defaults |
| `Returns` | Quantity or result type, units, and feasibility semantics |
| `Notes` | Equation, symbol definitions, unit of work, assumptions, and exclusions |
| `References` | A supporting source URL and bibliography key when available, or a concrete algebraic derivation for original accounting |
| `Examples` | A small executable example using the public API |

Put the reusable equation's full derivation in its physics function. A solver
should explain how it composes those equations and link to the relevant functions
using `See Also`. Avoid copying a derivation into several implementations.

Elementary identities do not need an unrelated citation. Use `Derivation:` in
`References` to explain how a result follows from its definitions, conservation
relationship, or stated construction. A heuristic must identify its assumed
relationship and limitations; labeling it a derivation does not make it a physical
law. Literature-derived methods should link the supporting source.

An equation or section number belongs in the reference only after checking the
source. A citation to a paper is not evidence that every constant in our
implementation came from it. Identify each addition as a modeling convention,
assumed efficiency, calibrated parameter, or algebraic consequence.

For example, the Roofline principle motivates taking the larger of compute and
memory time. An additive per-layer runtime tax is a separate assumption. Report
both, rather than attributing the entire implementation to the Roofline paper.

The existing provenance catalog records sources for values. Formula docstrings
record the derivation and modeling choices. These complement each other; a
verification-date field alone does not establish that an equation is correct.

## Keep scenario properties concise

Calculation scenarios share their inputs and assumptions across related properties.
Put the scenario's equation or composition map, assumptions, exclusions, sources,
and runnable example in its class docstring. A delegated scenario may name a
qualified `Implementation reference:` in `References`; the checker resolves every
linked target so a renamed solver cannot silently leave a broken explanation. Each public calculated property then
states what it means, its units, and its equation or the qualified function or
solver that owns the calculation. A simple alias can point to that contract instead
of repeating a derivation. A property that introduces additional arithmetic must
explain that arithmetic locally.

These property explanations are part of the code, not generated substitutes for
reading it. An extracted Python expression alone does not explain a unit of work,
a valid regime, or why a relation applies.

## Publish from the same source

The site already uses `quartodoc`, configured in `_quarto.yml`. Its NumPy docstring
parser turns code documentation into the [API reference](api/index.qmd).
The pre-render hook, `scripts/build_api.py`, regenerates the reference for a full
site build and checks public API coverage. Do not edit generated `docs/api/` pages.
The [scenario reference index](api/scenario-index.qmd) links class pages with
input fields, defaults, calculated properties, and their explanations. Single-page
previews do not regenerate the API; rebuild it explicitly when reviewing changed
docstrings.

From the package directory, with the development and documentation extras installed:

```bash
python docs/scripts/build_api.py
make modeling-docs-check
make docs
```

Keep conceptual explanations in Quarto guides and implementation contracts in
code. Link between them. Generate numerical tables from executable calculations;
[calibration and validation scope](empirical-calibration.md) is an example.
API coverage checks establish that pages exist, not that every explanation is complete.

## Enforce the convention

Run `make modeling-docs-check` from the package directory. This command is also
part of `make check`, the development and release CI workflows, and the local
pre-commit hooks. Install the development extra before running it.

| Check | What fails |
|---|---|
| Ruff with the NumPy pydocstyle convention | Missing or incorrectly formatted docstrings in the selected modules |
| Ruff formatter check | Python formatting that differs from the standard layout |
| numpydoc validation | Missing or misordered parameters, undocumented returns, malformed sections, or missing examples |
| MLSysIM contract check | Missing `Equation:`, `Assumptions:`, or `Excludes:` labels in `Notes`; missing supporting source URL, concrete `Derivation:`, or qualified `Implementation reference:` in `References` |
| Executable examples | A doctest fails or the examples contain no executable code |
| Citation-key check | A supplied key does not exist in the repository's paper bibliography |
| Equation display | Unquoted multiplication tokens could become Markdown emphasis instead of the written equation |
| Discovery | A newly added public calculation or scenario lacks its required contract |
| Scenario trace | A scenario property loses its local equation or link to an underlying contract |

The checker discovers public functions in the physics tree, public concrete
solver methods and helpers, generic Engine calculations, workload calculations,
calculated registry and result properties, serving profiles, constraint-explorer
calculations, and scenario classes and their public properties from source
definitions. New calculations in these modules enter the gate without someone
remembering to add an allowlist entry. Scenario definitions and result types are
scanned recursively through their domain packages, including base classes and
package initializers. The legacy `scenario_types.py` and `results.py` import
facades remain compatible entry points; imported aliases add no duplicate checks.
Discovery follows physical source definitions rather than historical `__module__`
values retained for serialization compatibility.
Private implementation modules, abstract interfaces, and presentation-only summary
methods are outside this numerical-contract inventory; their public callers own
the documented contract. Imported aliases are checked at the defining function.

`[tool.mlsysim.documentation]` in `pyproject.toml` controls optional module-wide
Ruff style and formatting checks and the numpydoc exceptions. It does not narrow
the discovered scientific-contract scope. Full NumPy contracts apply to equations
and solvers; scenario properties use the concise shared-context convention above.
Composition and conversion entry points have a separate ordinary NumPy API check:
parameters, return semantics, and executable examples, without artificial equations
or citations for dispatch and unit conversion. Presentation, serialization,
metadata lookup, schema/introspection, abstract interfaces, and optional backend
plumbing are not scientific-model contracts. Optional optimizer examples state
the required installation extra and are validated separately when it is present.

The only disabled numpydoc rules are the optional extended-summary and `See Also`
requirements. The scientific explanation belongs in `Notes`; cross-links remain
encouraged. The source distribution does not contain the paper bibliography, so
checks there explicitly report that key resolution is unavailable. Repository CI
checks the bibliography. A citation key existing does not prove that a source
supports an equation; that remains a review responsibility.

To apply formatting locally, run `python -m ruff format` on the affected modules.
Checks never rewrite files. The tests exercise both documented APIs and deliberate
failures such as an undocumented parameter, an unknown citation key, or an
incorrect example result. Tests also add new temporary calculations to prove
that discovery includes them, remove a scenario trace, and reject an empty or
unexplained source declaration.

The implementation uses standard [Ruff NumPy conventions](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#lint_pydocstyle_convention)
and [numpydoc validation](https://numpydoc.readthedocs.io/en/latest/validation.html).
It does not require changing the existing Quarto publishing system.

## Protect the textbook series

Treat a change to an equation, default, unit, or feasibility decision as a numerical
compatibility change even when the Python signature stays the same.

1. Record the old and new outputs with identical inputs and package versions.
2. Search consumers in **all four volumes**, including named scenarios and indirect
   solver calls. Include labs, slides, the paper, figures, and generated tables.
3. Execute affected textbook cells and compare the values interpolated into prose.
   Passing registry lookup tests alone does not check the claims around those values.
4. Review the surrounding claim: its inequality, bottleneck, comparison, and conclusion
   may change even when rounding hides a small numerical difference.
5. Flag prose discrepancies for a separate editorial decision. Do not silently rewrite
   a teaching claim or tune an equation merely to retain its previous answer.
6. Before a coordinated release, refresh approved generated artifacts and inspect
   the affected rendered pages and figures. Report any cells or environments not tested.

A structural cleanup should preserve outputs. A correctness fix may change them;
its release notes must explain the change. Neither passing tests nor agreement with
calibration cases establishes an accuracy guarantee for unseen workloads.
